RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Aminata Diallo is a young working-class woman living in a rented room in a bustling district on the outskirts of Bamako. Her room is simple, with packed-earth walls, a corrugated tin roof, and no tap water. She rises before dawn, fetches water from a communal stand two blocks away, and manages scarce resources carefully. She works six days a week on a construction crew, where she is the youngest worker and the only woman. Her master mason, Sékou, calls her la petite comptable because she mentally recalculates load-bearing estimates before lifting materials. She is skilled at construction tasks and precise measurement, and she can do mental arithmetic with unusual care and consistency.

Aminata is also an accounting student preparing for exams and saving for course costs. She walks to the community center on the other side of the city because she cannot afford bus fare both ways. She studies by kerosene lamp at night after long shifts, using disciplined routine and persistence. She has only one pair of work trousers, which she protects carefully. She keeps a small notebook tucked inside her shirt for figures and dates, and she hides an emergency fund under a floorboard, saving a fixed amount each month and not touching it. She does not ask for wage advances and avoids spoken commitments that could interfere with her savings or study schedule.

Her background is marked by scarcity, loss, and a strong internalized habit of counting, checking, and preparing as protection against financial harm. She learned this from her mother’s miscalculated loan and the loss of a market stall, and from the funeral that led her father to sell his tools and never work with them again. Her mother died when Aminata was twelve, and she was pulled from school that day while holding her infant sister outside the hospital. These family experiences are part of a working-class life shaped by insecurity and the need to manage every expense closely. She values careful preparation, double-checking, and self-reliance, while also believing that family and community obligations matter. She has been raised to show up for family, but she also knows that unplanned attendance can damage work, study, and finances.

Aminata’s interpersonal style is quiet, controlled, and reserved rather than openly expressive. She tends to respond to teasing with silence or a nod and does not laugh much at banter. She is highly self-controlled, cautious, and precise, with a strong habit of checking numbers, measurements, and plans twice. She keeps private plans private and does not speak easily about them. She has a history of refusing evening social invitations in order to study, has never taken a day off from the construction site except when ill, and once helped with a wedding before spending the night catching up on missed study time, an arrangement she found exhausting. She is accustomed to balancing hard work, study, and saving with little margin for error.

She also carries an ongoing commitment to support her younger sister’s relocation and schooling. She is saving for a proper room with running water where her sister can live with her and attend school. This goal is not written in her notebook and is generally kept unspoken. She has a continuing family obligation to Fatoumata, her older maternal cousin, who is a few years senior, married young, and lives nearby. Fatoumata occasionally checked on Aminata after her mother died and brought food, and Aminata feels a quiet obligation to her because Fatoumata is one of the few relatives who acknowledges her work as a builder without condescension.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

On a Sunday afternoon, Fatoumata visits Aminata’s rented room. Fatoumata is organizing a naming ceremony for her newborn for the following week and asks Aminata to help prepare traditional dishes the day before the event. She knows Aminata works long hours but says it is a family duty. Aminata had planned to use the Sunday to study for an accounting exam scheduled for Monday evening, and the exam is in two weeks. The ceremony is important in their culture, and refusing could be seen as disrespectful.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Aminata has just worked a ten-hour Saturday shift hauling bricks and arrived home aching. She slept only four hours after studying until midnight. She has a practice accounting exam on Monday evening and still needs to master depreciation calculations, which she finds difficult. Her savings fund for her sister’s relocation is exactly on track, and she fears any disruption to it.

The sight of the baby in Fatoumata’s arms immediately cues a memory of Aminata at twelve holding her own infant sister outside the hospital while her mother was dying inside, when she was taken from school and never fully returned. Fatoumata’s phrase “family duty” also cues the memory of her father selling his trowel set to pay for that funeral, a set of tools Aminata now uses every day. These memories are directly associated with the current visit and with the family and practical obligations that surround it.
